summary: Thariq Shihipar, who works on Claude Code at Anthropic, presents a field guide to Fable, the company's newest model. He compares Fable to milestone models like Sonnet 3.5, Opus 4, and Opus 4.5, framing the experience as an RPG map opening after the tutorial. The talk has four parts. Part one, unhobbling Claude, rests on the principle that models are grown, not designed. Capability overhang means models get smarter in spiky ways and tools determine which spikes are reachable—illustrated by the Pokemon 'aw' example where a chat model fails but Claude Code succeeds by writing a script. Anthropic removed 80 percent of Claude Code's system prompt because Fable-class models prefer context over constraints and are more imaginative than prior examples. The ask-user-question tool evolved from barely working on Opus 4 to generating embedded HTML questionnaires on Fable. Shihipar stresses this work is closer to biology than physics. Part two, finding your unknowns, uses a map-versus-territory framework. Techniques include blind spot passes for unknown unknowns, brainstorm-prototype sessions for unknown knowns in design, and Claude-led interviews. Additional tips include providing reference code as another map, asking Fable to log unknowns it encounters, and having Fable quiz the user to ensure understanding. Part three addresses the emotional shift: Shihipar recalls coding before LLMs as a foreign country of constant trade-offs, expresses grief over losing hand-coding joy, but insists the only way out is through. Part four, being unreasonable, draws on Anthropic's culture that tradeoffs are not real: good, fast, cheap should now be pick three. He built this presentation deck in four hours with Fable. He cautions that while building is easier, generating value remains hard, and closes by urging the audience to explore, make it real, and be less reasonable.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Fable announcement
sections.summary: Thariq introduces himself, takes a selfie per Claude Code tradition, and announces Fable is rolling out later that day. He compares Fable to memorable models like Sonnet 3.5 new, Opus 4, and Opus 4.5, and frames the talk as a field guide using an RPG open-world metaphor. The four parts are unhobbling Claude, finding your unknowns, dealing with the grief, and being unreasonable.

sections.title: Unhobbling Claude: models are grown, capability overhang
sections.summary: Models are grown not designed; the harness and prompt reflect human understanding of Claude. Capability overhang is introduced via the Pokemon 'aw' example: chat models fail despite knowing all Pokemon, but Claude Code writes a script to fetch and filter. Progression examples include giving models bash tools instead of relying on huge context, and Claude Tag working proactively in multiplayer.

sections.title: System prompt reduction and tool evolution
sections.summary: Anthropic removed 80% of Claude Code's system prompt because Fable-class models are more imaginative than the examples that previously constrained them, preferring context over constraints. The ask-user-question tool evolved from barely working on Opus 4, to 40-question interviews on Opus 4.5, to embedded HTML questionnaires on Fable. Shihipar emphasizes this is closer to biology than physics and recommends Anthropic's biology of a large language model paper.

sections.title: Finding your unknowns: map versus territory
sections.summary: The map is the plan, prompt, and spec; the territory is the actual codebase and real-world constraints. Unknowns are decision points not specified in the map. Shihipar introduces a matrix of known knowns, known unknowns, unknown knowns, and unknown unknowns, then describes techniques to surface them: blind spot passes, brainstorm-prototype sessions, and Claude-led interviews.

sections.title: Additional Fable tips: references, implementation notes, quizzing
sections.summary: Shihipar adds more tips for working with Fable: provide references such as existing code or HTML mock-ups as alternative maps, ask Fable to log unknowns it encounters so deviations can be traced, and have Fable quiz the user to verify understanding before creating a PR or merging. Staying in the loop is one of the most important practices.

sections.title: Dealing with the grief: emotional shift in coding productivity
sections.summary: Shihipar reflects on the emotional impact of Fable-class models. Coding before LLMs felt like a foreign country of constant trade-offs at his 30-person YC startup. He recalls both the joy of hand-coding and the misery of weeks-long debugging and swimming in failure. He cannot go back, and his resolution is that the only way out is through—staying engaged, unhobbling the model, and learning the new workflow.

sections.title: Being unreasonable: demand good, fast, and cheap
sections.summary: Shihipar's final part advocates being unreasonable. Anthropic's culture treats tradeoffs as not real; instead of prioritizing among good, fast, and cheap, demand all three. He built this presentation deck in about four hours with Fable. He cautions that building is easier but generating value remains hard, requiring many swings. He closes by urging the audience to go explore, make it real, and be less reasonable.
